title: A trillion-dollar market cap can't buy investment grade: Anthropic's bond issuance is likely junk-rated
excerpt: The stock market has pushed Anthropic to the trillion-dollar scale, but the bond market isn't buying it. The AI lab raised more than $100 billion last week and
content_html:
The stock market has pushed Anthropic to the trillion-dollar scale, but the bond market isn't buying it. The AI lab raised more than $100 billion last week and is valued at about $1.18 trillion, higher than Walmart and JPMorgan Chase; but it has committed roughly $900 billion over the coming years to buying compute, and Wall Street widely expects its bonds to be rated junk.

A Trillion-Dollar Valuation, a BB Rating

Bond fund managers generally expect its rating to fall in the BB range, one to two notches below investment grade. It would then become the largest high-yield issuer in the U.S. by market value—the record holder, Hilton, is only about $80 billion.

Osterweis fund manager Manchak's question is blunt: How do you price a company that has committed to spending $900 billion? CEO Amodei responded on Thursday, "I hope that one day we will get an investment-grade rating." The payoff would also be big: investment grade would mean access to the $8.6 trillion high-grade bond market. Broadcom and Nvidia have already guaranteed tens of billions of dollars for chip buyers and are counting on AI labs to issue bonds independently to untangle the circular financing deadlock.

A Three-Year Window

Analysts estimate that the company has $96 billion in cash. Together with an IPO and private fundraising, that is enough to cover more than a year of spending, and about half of its commitments do not come due until after 2030. Building its own compute hardware could also help it earn a rating, much as SpaceX did with its satellite business. But the window is only about three years; if it still fails to meet the standard by then, repayment pressure will be enormous.

After former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departed, the chip-guarantee business he championed may shrink; some of the $25 billion in bonds SpaceX issued in June have already fallen more than 10%, and fund managers' appetite for such assets has peaked. Apollo's Rowan made a stinging point: between that market value and a 16% to 18% bond issuance yield, one valuation has to be wrong.
